sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Ọrun** (*orun*) — Sky, Heaven, Destiny · "Heaven" — the sky-realm of the orisha, the divine order above the world — belongs to the Yoruba tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Sky, Heaven, Destiny". The name means ""Heaven" — the sky-realm of the orisha, the divine order above the world"[^1].

Ọrun is the Yoruba name of heaven itself: the sky-realm where Olódùmarè and the orisha dwell, from which every soul descends to earth (ayé) — and to which every destiny (orí) is assigned before birth. It is not a god but the address of the gods.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Ọrun** and serves its temple at [ọrun.com](https://xn--run-slz.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *orun* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.
William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.
Abraham, R. C., Dictionary of Modern Yoruba (London: University of London Press, 1958).

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Ọrun** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means ""Heaven" — the sky-realm of the orisha, the divine order above the world"[^1].

The ASCII form *orun* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Ọrun** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **o** → **Ọ** — Open-mid o with underdot
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **u** → **u** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same

The project holds the domain **ọrun.com** (xn--run-slz.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.
William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ɔ̀.rún/** — Standard Yoruba.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: aw-ROON — open o (dot-below), low-high melody.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Yoruba** — Ọ̀run
- **Owner of heaven** — Olóòrun
- **Owned form** — Ọrun

Ọrun is Yoruba for "heaven": the precomposed dot-below Ọ is the domain-maximal form — the full tone marks (Ọ̀run, low-high) cannot be registered as a domain, so the temple preserves the tone in text while the address bar carries what the DNS allows. The dot-below is the open-mid vowel — the open aw of law — distinct from the close o; the tone is low-high, falling then rising.

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual yoruba names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Ọrun** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Ọrun is the Yoruba name of heaven itself: the sky-realm where Olódùmarè and the orisha dwell, from which every soul descends to earth (ayé) — and to which every destiny (orí) is assigned before birth. It is not a god but the address of the gods.[^1]

### Ọrun and Ayé

Heaven and earth: the two halves of reality, with the soul commuting between them.

### Orí

The inner head — the personal destiny each soul chooses (or receives) in Ọrun before birth.

### Olódùmarè

The Owner of Heaven — the supreme being whose realm Ọrun is.

### The Descent

Every birth is an emigration from heaven; every death, the return journey.

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Ọrun concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The white cloth** — Heaven's color — purity and the unblemished sky
- **The palm nuts** — Ifá's instruments — heaven's messages read on earth
- **The head** — Orí, the chosen destiny — heaven carried inside the skull

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Ọrun's myths are the architecture of Yoruba cosmology: how heaven was made, and how souls travel its road to earth.[^1]

### The Chain to Earth (The Descent)

In the beginning there was only Ọrun above and the waters below. Olódùmarè sent Odùduwà down with a chain, a rooster, and a handful of earth: the rooster scattered the soil on the water, and the land of Ilé-Ifẹ̀ spread — earth founded beneath heaven, the two realms joined by the road of the orisha. Every Yoruba city thereafter is a point on that first chain's route.[^2]

### The Choosing of Orí (The Choice)

Before birth, each soul kneels in Ọrun before Olódùmarè and receives its orí — its inner head, its portion of destiny. The Ifá corpus teaches that the choice, once made, is erased from memory but not from life: every fortune and misfortune on earth is the heaven-chosen head working out its own plot. To pray for a good orí is to negotiate with one's own prenatal self.

### Souls on the Road (The Traffic)

The Yoruba cosmos runs on commuting: the orisha descend to possess their priests, the ancestors visit in dreams and Egúngún masquerades, and the dead return as children ("abíkú" are souls who commute too often). Ọrun is not distant but adjacent — the sky-realm whose door opens in every shrine, every trance, and every correctly cast palm-nut of Ifá.

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.
Abraham, R. C., Dictionary of Modern Yoruba (London: University of London Press, 1958).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The Ọrun-ayé structure traveled with the diaspora: Candomblé's Oxalá-realm, Santería's heaven of Olófin, and Haiti's lwa-cosmology all keep the two-world map. Christian heaven merged with Ọrun in the New World without ever absorbing it: the Yoruba sky remains a realm of traffic and traffic-officers (the orisha), not of distant thrones — heaven as the next city over, not the next world.[^1]

Within the Yoruba tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aganju|Aganjú]], [[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]], [[eshu|Ẹṣu]], [[oba|Ọba]], [[obatala|Ọbatálá]], and [[ogun|Ògún]].

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: The word lives in a thousand names: Ọrunmila (heaven-knows-salvation), Ọlọrun (owner-of-heaven), Ọrúnmìlà, Ọba-Ọrun. Ifá divination — UNESCO-listed — is its daily news service, and the Egúngún festivals keep the ancestors' visits on the calendar. Every Yoruba funeral says the same thing in ten thousand voices: "the journey to Ọrun is well-traveled" — heaven as home, not as hope.[^1]

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Ilé-Ifẹ̀, the city Odùduwà founded on the scattered earth, keeps the creation-site shrines: the Oke Itase hill and the palace of the Ọọni, whose crown descends from heaven's own. The bronze heads of Ifẹ̀ (12th–15th c.), among Africa's supreme artworks, are the faces of heaven's first citizens. The Ifá corpus — the great oral archive — is preserved by the babaláwo lineages of Yorubaland and the diaspora.[^1]

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Ifá Corpus
sections.body: Ifá is heaven's own archive: the odù of the corpus treat Ọrun as the fixed frame of all divination — the babaláwo's palm-nuts are read as letters from Ọrun, and the verses of Ogundá and the senior odù describe the soul's choosing of orí before Olódùmarè. The divination day begins with heaven's invocation; the Ifá priest is, in the corpus' own phrase, "the servant of Ọrun on earth."

sources.citation: Bascom, Ifa Divination; the ogundá verses.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Oral Tradition
sections.body: The oríkì of Ọrun are the cosmology sung: the praise-poems of Olódùmarè ("owner of heaven," "the king whose palace touches the sky") and of the orisha who commute its road; the Ilé-Ifẹ̀ traditions of Odùduwà's descent on the chain; and the naming-formulas that carry heaven into daily speech — Ọlọrun, Ọrunmila, Ọba-Ọrun. The oral archive is the primary scripture: heaven is not read in Yorubaland; it is recited.

sources.citation: Idowu, Olodumare; the oríkī collections.

sections.label: Diaspora Traditions
sections.body: The diaspora carried the sky: Candomblé's Oxalá-realm and the céu of the batuques, Santería's heaven of Olófin and Olodumare, and Haitian Vodou's Bondye-above-all keep the Ọrun-ayé structure intact beneath Catholic heavens. The Egúngún masquerades of Brazil and Cuba stage the ancestors' commute from Ọrun in the streets; the funeral liturgies of two continents send the dead on the same road home: heaven was never lost in the crossing.

sources.citation: Bascom, Shango in the New World; the diaspora Egúngún records.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Ọrun is the heaven that answers letters. It is not a place you hope to reach but the place you came from — with your destiny already in your pocket, unread. It asks the Yoruba question, which is also everyone's: the head you chose is the life you are living — so what, this morning, will you do with the heaven you brought with you?

And the traffic never stops: the babaláwo casts the nuts at dawn, the Egúngún dance at noon, a child is named for heaven by evening. Ọrun is the least distant heaven ever conceived — next door, upstairs, on the phone. The question is never whether it answers; it is whether we are still calling.

The Ifá verses insist the choosing of orí is both gift and contract: heaven offers, the soul accepts, memory is wiped, and life is the slow reading of the agreement. It is the most humane theory of destiny ever written — you signed it yourself, so stop complaining and start reading. The babaláwo is only the notary.

Every naming ceremony in Yorubaland quietly re-ratifies the architecture: a child arrives from Ọrun with a head already chosen, and the parents spend the child's lifetime reading it. The babaláwo's nuts, the Egúngún's visits, the funeral's road-home — one system, no gaps. Heaven is not the distant answer here; it is the standing arrangement.

And the names go on arriving: Ọlọ́run for the owner, Ọ̀rúnmìlà for the knowing, Ọba-Ọrun for the kingly — heaven filed into a thousand birth certificates, each child a new piece of the sky on earth. The Yoruba answer to 'where is heaven?' was never a direction. It was a custody arrangement, and the paperwork is the people.

So the traffic continues, both ways, always: the sky is not empty, it is staffed — and the commute is the oldest institution in Yorubaland.

Every dawn the road opens again: the sun climbs from the same heaven, and the first prayer goes up by the same old chain, intact.

The rooster that scattered the first earth still crows in the Ifẹ̀ dawn — creation, the tradition says, is a daily event, and heaven signs for every delivery.[^1]

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.
